title: Trump and NYT Say There’s a Russian Spy Base in Cuba. Turns Out, It’s a School.

_This story was written in collaboration with**[Belly of the
Beast](https://www.bellyofthebeastcuba.com/)** , an independent media outlet
that covers Cuba and U.S.-Cuba relations. You can support their work on
[Patreon](https://www.patreon.com/cw/BellyoftheBeastCuba)._

Since U.S. President Donald Trump imposed an executive order in January
threatening tariffs on any country that ships fuel to Cuba, major media
outlets have descended on the island to report on the resulting [prolonged
blackouts](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=26932413849731765), [collapsing
hospitals](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/cuba/inside-cuba-hospital-outages-
hard-hit-blackouts-rcna264184), and [piles of uncollected
trash](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/may/07/rubbish-
health-cuba-us-oil-blockade-waste-collection-fuel-crisis-havana).

Far less attention has been paid to the rationale the administration offered
for imposing the blockade in the first place.

The [executive order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-
actions/2026/01/addressing-threats-to-the-united-states-by-the-government-of-
cuba/) states that Cuba represents a "national emergency" and poses an
"unusual and extraordinary threat" to the United States, stringing together a
kitchen-sink list of familiar allegations, including accusations that Cuba
sponsors terrorism and aligns itself with "dangerous adversaries" of the
United States, such as Iran, Hamas, Russia, and China.

More specifically, the order claims that "Cuba hosts Russia's largest overseas
signals intelligence facility, which tries to steal sensitive national
security information of the United States."

For two months, the allegation that Cuba was hosting a major Russian spy base
was largely ignored by U.S. media outlets. Then, on March 24, The New York
Times published an[
article](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/24/us/politics/cuba-russia-
china.html) by Michael Crowley claiming not only that the Russian spy base
exists, but that it "bristles with antennas and other eavesdropping equipment"
capable of spying on the U.S. Central Command, the satellite launchpads of
Cape Canaveral, and Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence.

Crowley [pinpointed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/14/us/politics/cia-
director-visits-cuba.html) the location: a former Soviet base on the outskirts
of Havana called Lourdes that was "temporarily shut" by Vladimir Putin in 2001
but was reopened in 2014, according to the Times.

There is just one problem with this story: the base isn't there.

The State Department did not respond to a request for comment. Belly of the
Beast also sent requests to The New York Times and to Michael Crowley but
received no response.

Today, Lourdes (also known as Torrens) is home to Cuba's University of
Computer Sciences (UCI). [The reporting team at Belly of the
Beast](https://www.bellyofthebeastcuba.com/this-russian-base-in-cuba-is-
spying-on-you)**** spent the better part of two days walking the campus,
searching the grounds, and speaking with students, faculty, and workers. We
found no evidence of an active Russian intelligence base, much less the sort
of extensive equipment described by the Times.

"Do I look like a Russian spy?" laughed Malcolm Jarrozai, a 40-year-old art
professor who has been teaching at UCI and living at a residence on campus
since 2006. "It's truly laughable that these kinds of claims are being made
and that major outlets like The New York Times give them a platform and allow
them to be used to justify policies against Cuba."

## **The Rise and Fall of Lourdes**

Construction of a Soviet signals intelligence (SIGINT) facility in Cuba[
began](https://irp.fas.org/imint/c80_04.htm) as early as 1962, even before the
Cuban Missile Crisis. By the 1980s,[
](https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP04T00794R000100080001-0.pdf)U.S.
intelligence said Lourdes [was](https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-
RDP04T00794R000100080001-0.pdf) "the USSR's largest and most valuable base
outside the Soviet Union for intelligence collection against the United
States."

In a 1983 televised address, President Ronald Reagan[
cited](https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/address-nation-defense-
and-national-security) Lourdes as evidence of the Soviet threat to argue
against proposed congressional budget cuts to defense spending. Reagan said
the 28-square-mile base was manned by [1,500 Soviet technicians
](https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP81B00401R000300020017-2.pdf)and
had grown by 60 percent in the previous decade. Two years later, the
Departments of State and Defense[
estimated](https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-
RDP88B00745R000100140026-6.pdf) there were as many as 14,700 Soviet personnel
in Cuba, including 2,100 at Lourdes.

Even after the fall of the Soviet Union, the Lourdes base remained in place to
the consternation of neoconservatives and Cuban-American hardliners. In 1998,
Jane's Intelligence Review[ wrote](https://www.congress.gov/committee-
report/106th-congress/house-report/668/1) that Lourdes remained "the greatest
single overseas GRU [Russian military intelligence] asset" and[
provided](https://jamestown.org/clinton-administration-not-opposed-to-russian-
spy-facility-in-cuba-u-s/) 60-70 percent of Russian electronic intelligence
data on the United States. Two years later, a congressional report noted that[
there were](https://www.congress.gov/committee-report/106th-congress/house-
report/668/1) still more than 1,500 Russian engineers, technicians and
military personnel at the base.

In January 2001, the hardline anti-Castro lawmaker Rep. Ileana Ros-Lehtinen
(R-FL)[ introduced a
bill](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/RL/PDF/RL30806/RL30806.5.pdf)
that would have prohibited forgiveness of Russian government debt until
Lourdes was shuttered. Ten months later, Ros-Lehtinen, for whom Marco Rubio[
served as an intern](https://rollcall.com/2015/04/06/when-jeb-bush-managed-a-
house-campaign) in the early 1990s, got her wish.

On October 17, 2001, Russia's President Vladimir Putin[
announced](https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/2001/10/18/726290.html)
that Russia would abandon Lourdes. U.S. President George W. Bush[
congratulated](https://georgewbush-
whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2001/10/20011017-10.html) Putin for
taking down a "Cold War relic" and hailed the news as "another indication that
the Cold War is over."

But other U.S. politicians have had a harder time letting go of the Cold War.

## **From Russia to China**

The closure of Lourdes didn't end talk of foreign spy bases in Cuba. Even
before the Russians finally handed the base over to Cuban authorities in
August 2002, El Nuevo Herald published [an
article](https://www.cubanet.org/htdocs/CNews/y02/jun02/12o4.htm) claiming
that Lourdes had been replaced by a Chinese base at Bejucal, a town about
seven miles away.

But allegations that China was using Cuba to spy on the United States did not
become a national news story until 2023, when The Wall Street Journal __[
reported](https://www.wsj.com/world/cuba-to-host-secret-chinese-spy-base-
focusing-on-u-s-b2fed0e0) that the two countries had reached a "secret
agreement" for China to establish a spy base in Cuba. The Journal, citing
anonymous officials "familiar with highly classified intelligence," said China
had agreed "in principle" to pay Cuba "several billion dollars to allow it to
build an eavesdropping station," and described the agreement as a "brash new
geopolitical challenge" that has "sparked alarm" in the Biden administration.

A year later, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)
released a[ report](https://features.csis.org/hiddenreach/china-cuba-spy-
sigint/) that used commercial satellite imagery to identify four locations in
Cuba, including Bejucal, "where China is most likely operating" its alleged
spy bases.

The report, which was part of CSIS's "Hidden Reach" program to expose China's
influence around the world, provided no evidence that the alleged spy bases in
Cuba, even if real, were being operated by China. CSIS [recently
acknowledged](https://www.csis.org/analysis/new-activity-possible-chinese-
intelligence-facilities-cuba) there was "no clear publicly available evidence"
proving China's presence at Bejucal.

"The report pulls the rumors and speculation in only one direction--to support
its preordained conclusion that Chinese intelligence capabilities are
expanding in ways threatening to U.S. interests, with Cuba's full support,"
said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst who also served as the nation's
top intelligence officer on Latin America. "That's bad analysis."

Belly of the Beast [attempted to
visit](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n4uVFE-n4lw) three of the four
locations identified in the CSIS report. They appeared to be Cuban military
installations but we found no evidence of heightened security or Chinese
personnel.

At one site, the guard posts appeared abandoned. Part of the facility's
perimeter was lined with a rusty fence. Another section was bordered by trees.
The main entrance was guarded by an elderly Cuban woman who was an unarmed
civilian employed by Cuba's Vigilance and Protection Corps (CVP), a state
agency that provides security services at schools, hospitals, stores, and
hotels.

At another site, antennas draped in ivy and a dirt-covered satellite dish
could be seen from the street.

"That's laughably old technology," said Armstrong after viewing video footage
from two of the facilities. "It's sort of an insult to the Chinese if you're
going to say that this is the future of their intel collection against the
United States."

CSIS claimed the fourth location, near Santiago de Cuba, was being used to
construct a circularly disposed antenna array (CDAA), a Cold War-era
technology that [has become largely
obsolete](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7iiBN7If9uQ). The report itself
acknowledges that Russia and the United States have abandoned most of their
CDAAs.

A CSIS update to the report [published last
month](https://www.csis.org/analysis/new-activity-possible-chinese-
intelligence-facilities-cuba) said construction had "largely ceased" and there
was no indication the site was operational.

The CSIS report made no mention of a Russian spy base beyond noting that
Lourdes had operated during the Cold War.

But Lourdes had nonetheless resurfaced in the news in 2014 amid heightened
U.S.-Russian tensions, when The New York Times
[reported](https://www.nytimes.com/2014/07/17/world/americas/russia-to-reopen-
spying-post-in-cuba.html) that Russia had plans to reopen the base, [citing a
Russian newspaper](https://www.kommersant.ru/doc/2525998) and Russian
parliamentarians who "appeared to confirm the report." The next day, Putin
[said](https://www.voanews.com/a/putin-denies-cuba-spy-base-
reopening/1959682.html) Russia had no such plans.

Not much was heard about the purported spy base until Trump's executive order
revived the narrative that the Russians had returned to Cuba, though Rubio did
mention Lourdes at a [2016 Republican primary
debate](https://www.cnn.com/2016/03/10/politics/republican-debate-transcript-
full-text) against Trump in Miami: "Here's a good deal…Cuba kicks out the
Russians from Lourdes and kicks out the Chinese listening station in Bejucal."

In June [testimony](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-H50QxEApYg) before the
Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Rubio was asked for evidence supporting
Cuba's designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.

"Cuba continues to host a pretty substantial collection of intelligence sites
on behalf of the Chinese and the Russians," he said.

## **From Spy Base to Cuba 's Silicon Valley**

Cuban engineer Rafael Torralbas first stepped foot on the Russian base in
April 2002. Torralbas and two other colleagues were tasked with creating a
university within a matter of months.

"We had the challenge of receiving the installations being left behind by the
Russian officials," said Torralbas. "There were huge [satellite dish]
antennas, and I witnessed the process of dismantling them. There was
technological equipment connected to the antennas, which we never saw. We knew
it had been there, but the Russian officials had dismantled it all and they
handed over the buildings completely empty."

Torralbas said the Russians removed "absolutely every antenna" along with
everything else, including furniture and curtains. The Russians hauled the
base's equipment home in six Antonov An-124 Ruslan cargo plane flights,
according to Torralbas.

On September 23, 2002, one month after the last Russian left Lourdes, the
University of Computer Sciences held its first classes on the grounds of the
old base, which is located just two miles from Havana's Jose Marti
International Airport.

In the following years, some of the Russian buildings were torn down, while
others were repurposed. The apartment buildings housing the Russian personnel
and their families were converted into residences for students and professors.
A daycare center became a center for medical technology. A supermarket was
turned into a library.

Torralbas now serves as the president of the[ Havana Science and Technology
Park](https://www.3ce.cu/), an innovation hub on the UCI campus that he says
was inspired by Silicon Valley. Founded in 2020, the Technology Park serves as
an incubator for Cuban tech startups, most of them private companies (despite[
claims to the contrary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WY_FULnHtpA) by hard-
line politicians in Florida, Cuba's private sector has been thriving in recent
years). The park also provides technological support to foreign and state-run
companies.

Torralbas says the idea that Lourdes was reopened "could only exist in the
mind of the person who made up that news."

"At no time, in this university, has anything existed that is not school
buildings, students, computer science development centers, postgrad programs,
that is, the normal activities of a university," he said. "It's shocking to me
that someone in the intelligence community in the United States, with access
to satellite images, could claim that a [spy base] exists here now."

## **Hunting for Russian Spies**

We spent hours walking around UCI's expansive tree-lined campus and drove
around the perimeter, looking for any signs of signals intelligence or
military installations. The security presence was minimal. We moved around
freely and nobody seemed to care who we were or what we were doing. There was
a guard at the entrance and two others in a far corner of the campus, where
they watched over what appeared to be a side entrance--a partially closed door
made of corrugated metal. The guards, who were unarmed, said they worked for a
state-run security company. There were no military checkpoints.

According to Torralbas, more than 80% of the buildings on the campus were
built since the Russians left 24 years ago. New classroom buildings, computer
labs and research centers now occupy land where Soviet antennas once stood.

The only remnant of the old base we came across was a crumbling watchtower
near the perimeter of the campus. It was impossible to ascend as its metal
ladder had long since rusted away, leaving a small piece still visible at the
top.

As for The New York Times' claim that the re-opened Lourdes "bristles with
antennas"--we ultimately found two mobile phone antennas belonging to ETECSA,
the state telecommunications company.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Avno!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F08286728-5ff8-4332-8480-c888dbe20b8f_4032x3024.jpeg)_One
of the only antennas that is visible at the university. University staff say
it is a mobile phone antenna owned by Cuba 's state-run telecommunications
company. Photo: Reed Lindsa_

"We're in a rural area, so this is the only way we can have service for phone
calls, text messages, internet, and everything else," explained Hector
Gonzalez, a UCI graduate who now works in its communications department. "The
antennas that were here [under the Russians] that were dismantled were
different. They were enormous satellite dishes that you can see in some old
photos, giant radars many meters high. These are just ordinary mobile network
antennas."

The campus was mostly deserted. There are more than 2,500 undergraduate
students currently enrolled at UCI, but only a handful were on campus.

The oil blockade has ground Cuba's public transportation to a halt. In
February, with students and professors unable to get to class, Cuba's
universities shifted to remote and hybrid instruction, suspending most in-
person classes.

"It's a shame our students aren't here today," said Aylin Estrada, a UCI
graduate and now a university dean who guided us around one of the newer
school buildings, which has dozens of classrooms. "Normally these hallways are
full of students, smiling, learning."

"Those buildings over there used to be for the people who worked [on the
base]," said Franklin Quintana, a 37-year-old software developer, pointing to
faded green five-story apartment buildings that now house university staff.

Quintana, who recently returned to the university to work as a software
developer, shook his head when asked about the spy base.

"It's a false justification. There's no other way to understand it," he said.

"Rubio should come and look for it himself then. Look for it and prove it's
here," said 68-year-old Estrella Luque, a school administrator whose daughter
and son graduated from UCI and are now professors. "Cuba isn't a threat to
anyone. I don't think anyone with two brain cells to rub together believes
that."

After watching her children study and later teach at the university, Luque
said she was sad to see the campus without students.

"They can say we're a failed state if they want…but no one can ignore or deny
the impact of the blockade," said Luque. "A country like this little island,
which has virtually no natural resources--we're not a major oil-producing
island or a country with abundant resources--if you don't let oil in,
naturally everything starts to fall apart. That's what's happening to us. But
here we are. We keep going."
